newsitem.title: UK: Fate of Britain's big Millennium project in doubt.
newsitem.headline: Fate of Britain's big Millennium project in doubt.

text.p: The fate of the centrepiece of Britain's plans to celebrate the Millennium was in the balance on Thursday after inconclusive top-level talks between the government and the main opposition Labour party.

Deputy Prime Minister Michael Heseltine met Labour leader Tony Blair to try to persuade Labour, hot favourites to win the forthcoming election, to give its approval to plans for a 750 million pound ($1.26 billion) exhibition at Greenwich, London.
Backers of the project, at the heart of which is a huge dome to be built on reclaimed land, say time is running out.
They fear business sponsors will pull out if Labour does not endorse it unequivocally now.
Labour officials said the 25-minute meeting at the House of Commons had been good-natured and had cleared the air.

But it failed to overcome the main stumbling block -- Labour's insistence on including in a parliamentary statement by the government its right to review the project if it wins power and to ensure it comes in on budget.
Labour's heritage spokesman, Jack Cunningham, angrily rejected charges that he was jeopardising the project by dragging his feet.
"We have never prevaricated," he told reporters, adding that he had bent over backwards to make the scheme a success.
He said Labour was fully committed to a first-class exhibition but it was only reasonable that it should have the right to review the project if it takes office.

Cunningham said this safeguard was especially necessary because the project would rely on 400 million pounds from the national lottery and still had a cash shortfall in its draft budget of more than 200 million pounds.
Labour officials said ministers were reluctant to concede in an official statement to parliament even the possibility that Labour would win the election.
